chapters.title: Chapter 3: Gold as a Macro Hedge

lessons.title: Gold, Real Interest Rates, and the Dollar

children.text: Two Engines, Usually Pointed the Same Way

The previous lesson named real interest rates as gold's single biggest fundamental driver. There is a second engine sitting right next to it: the US dollar. Gold is priced globally in dollars, so a weaker dollar mechanically makes gold cheaper for anyone holding euros, yen or rupees, which tends to pull in more buying. Most of the time, these two engines point the same direction, because the same US Federal Reserve decisions that move real rates also move the dollar. This lesson shows how each one works on its own, what happens on the rare occasions they pull apart, and why the dollar channel matters twice as much for an Indian investor as it does for a US one.

body.text: Gold competes against two things at once: the yield you give up by not holding a bond, and the currency you're pricing it in. Most gold moves are one, or both, of these two things, not something happening to gold itself.

children.text: How to Actually Track Real Rates

The standard market proxy for the real interest rate that matters to gold is the yield on US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, TIPS, typically the 10-year maturity. Unlike a normal Treasury bond, a TIPS yield already strips out expected inflation, so it is a direct, market-priced read on the real rate rather than something you have to estimate yourself.

children.text: When the Relationship Held, and When It Didn't

body.title: Gold and Real Rates: A Real Case Study

events.title: Real Yields Turn Deeply Negative
events.description: Pandemic-era rate cuts and bond buying pushed US real yields firmly negative. Gold responded exactly as the framework predicts, closing above $2,000 an ounce for the first time that August.

events.title: The Fastest Rate-Hiking Cycle in Decades
events.description: As the Fed raised rates aggressively to fight inflation, real yields swung from firmly negative to solidly positive within roughly a year. Gold dipped but held up far better than the simple real-rate framework alone would have predicted.

events.title: Record Highs Despite Positive Real Rates
events.description: Gold went on to set fresh record highs even with real yields staying positive, a period that overlapped with heavy central bank buying, described in the previous lesson, and elevated geopolitical risk. The 'normal' relationship had clearly broken down.

body.text: Real rates explain a large share of gold's medium-term direction, but not all of it, and definitely not all of the time. When central bank buying or acute crisis demand is strong enough, gold can rise alongside rising real rates for an extended period. Treat the real-rate framework as your default lens, not a mechanical trading rule.

children.text: Why the Dollar Channel Matters Twice as Much for an Indian Investor

Chapter 2 showed that a weaker rupee and a rising oil price compound each other into a double tax on India. Gold has the mirror-image version of the same mechanic, and for an Indian holder it usually works the other way: as a tailwind, not a tax.

body.caption: The same multiplication from Chapter 2's oil lesson, but this time the second variable tends to help rather than hurt, since the rupee has depreciated fairly steadily against the dollar over the long run.

children.text: This is why gold measured in rupees has historically delivered a smoother, and often higher, long-run return than gold measured in dollars: Indian holders pick up the international gold price move and the rupee's gradual depreciation, stacked on top of each other, rather than one offsetting the other.

body.title: Work the Rupee Tailwind
body.prompt: International gold prices rise 8% over a year in dollar terms, while the rupee depreciates 4% against the dollar over the same period. Approximately what is the total return for an Indian investor holding gold, measured in rupees?
body.explanation: The two effects multiply: 1.08 times 1.04, minus 1, works out to approximately 12.3%, noticeably higher than the 8% dollar-denominated gain alone, because the rupee depreciation adds to the return instead of subtracting from it.

body.label: Gold's First Close Above $2,000/oz
body.context: A landmark moment that came during a period of deeply negative US real yields, and a clean textbook example of the real-rate relationship working exactly as this lesson describes.

points: Gold's two biggest fundamental engines are real interest rates, tracked via the US 10-year TIPS yield, and the US dollar, tracked via the Dollar Index.

The relationship held cleanly in 2020, when negative real yields coincided with gold's first close above $2,000 an ounce, but broke down between 2022 and 2024, when gold rallied to record highs despite positive real yields, driven by central bank buying and geopolitical demand.
For an Indian investor, rupee depreciation against the dollar has historically added to gold returns rather than subtracting from them, the mirror image of the oil double-tax effect from Chapter 2.

Use real rates and the dollar as your default lens on gold, but hold that view loosely: the next lesson turns this into a practical framework for actually building gold exposure in an Indian portfolio.
